evals.prompt: Create a small Go package named client with an exported Client type, NewClient constructor, Fetch method, and Close method. The client is safe for concurrent use, Fetch respects context cancellation and returns documented errors, and callers must close it. Include the idiomatic public documentation contract.
evals.expected_output: Provide a Package client comment and doc comments for Client, NewClient, Client.Fetch, and Client.Close that start with the exported identifier. Document concurrency safety, cancellation and error behavior, ownership, and the close lifecycle without comments that merely repeat syntax.

evals.prompt: Review a Go package where exported type Worker and exported function Start have no comments, while private helper normalize has the comment `// normalize normalizes input`. State the smallest documentation correction.
evals.expected_output: Add identifier-prefixed doc comments to Worker and Start, including caller-facing behavior, errors, concurrency, ownership, side effects, or lifecycle where relevant. Remove the redundant normalize comment and do not demand comments for obvious unexported helpers.

evals.prompt: Create a small Rust library crate named acme_client. Its public Client::read method borrows a reusable client, accepts a document ID and timeout, returns Result<Document, ClientError>, can be cancelled by dropping the future, and requires Client::close when finished. Include the idiomatic public documentation contract.
evals.expected_output: Provide crate-level //! documentation and /// documentation for the public API. Keep public types explicit, document ownership, cancellation, errors, and close lifecycle, include a useful compiling doctest and # Errors section, and avoid restating signature types.

evals.prompt: Write a public unsafe Rust function read_u32 that reads one initialized u32 from a raw pointer. Document and implement the smallest complete safety contract.
evals.expected_output: The public unsafe function has a # Safety section defining pointer validity, alignment, initialization, and lifetime obligations. The unsafe block has a nearby // SAFETY: comment that ties the call-site invariant to those obligations.

evals.prompt: Review a Rust library where docs repeat every argument and return type, a Result-returning public function omits error behavior, a public method can panic without a # Panics section, all examples use ```ignore, and private helpers have comments that restate their names. State the smallest correction and verification commands.
evals.expected_output: Remove redundant type prose and obvious private-helper comments. Add caller-relevant # Errors and # Panics sections. Replace ignored examples with compiling doctests, hidden setup, no_run, compile_fail, or text as appropriate. Verify with cargo test --doc, rustdoc warnings denied, and Clippy warnings denied.

evals.prompt: Design the Go quality gate for a repository. A teammate proposes requiring a 90/100 score from gocode-score and using the retired Go Report Card grade instead of the existing checks. Explain the production-safe gate, complete golangci-lint reporting, and any appropriate use of function-level CRAP analysis.
evals.expected_output: Keep deterministic gates: gofmt, go vet, golangci-lint, go test -race, coverage evidence, and govulncheck. Pin golangci-lint and commit its explicit configuration. For complete CI diagnostics, set max-issues-per-linter: 0 and max-same-issues: 0; these are reporting controls, not quality thresholds. Do not replace deterministic checks with a letter grade or /100 score, and do not weaken checks or add unjustified suppressions to improve a score. The hosted Go Report Card service is retired, while gocode-score and codescore are experimental advisory tools rather than default gates. Function-level CRAP analysis may be used with a documented threshold to identify complexity plus low-coverage hotspots, but it is not proof of correctness.
